content: The benefits and potential risks of discontinuing versus continuing antiviral therapy postpartum should be carefully evaluated. This includes monitoring fibrosis progression using non-invasive tests at regular intervals after childbirth. Additionally, the feasibility and effectiveness of integrated and simplified service delivery models for antenatal hepatitis B care and treatment, as well as the triple elimination of HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B, should be assessed. Recommendations for Treating Adolescents with Chronic Hepatitis B (CHB) Treatment is recommended for all adolescents aged 12–17 years, including pregnant and non-pregnant adolescent girls of reproductive age, who meet the following criteria: 1. Evidence of significant fibrosis or cirrhosis (≥5 kPa on transient elastography), regardless of HBV DNA or ALT levels (strong recommendation, low-certainty evidence). 2. HBV DNA levels >2000 IU/mL and ALT levels above the upper limit of normal (ULN) (30 U/L for males and 19 U/L for females) (conditional recommendation, low-certainty evidence). 3. Presence of co-infections (e.g., HIV, HDV, HCV), family history of liver cancer or cirrhosis, immune suppression (e.g., long-term steroids, organ or stem cell transplant), comorbidities (e.g., diabetes, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, iron overload), or extrahepatic manifestations (e.g., glomerulonephritis, vasculitis), regardless of APRI score, HBV DNA, or ALT levels (conditional recommendation, low-certainty evidence). Persistent HBsAg for six months or more defines CHB in adolescents and children. Clinical features of decompensated cirrhosis include ascites, variceal hemorrhage, hepatic encephalopathy, coagulopathy, or jaundice. Other signs of advanced liver disease or cirrhosis may include hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, pruritus, fatigue, arthralgia, palmar erythema, and edema. Antiviral Therapy for Adolescents and Children Preferred antiviral regimens for adolescents and children include nucleos(t)ide analogues with a high genetic barrier to resistance, such as tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) or entecavir (ETV). TDF combined with lamivudine (3TC) or emtricitabine (FTC) is recommended as an alternative regimen when TDF monotherapy is unavailable. For individuals with osteoporosis or impaired kidney function, entecavir or tenofovir alafenamide fumarate (TAF) is recommended. TAF is also an alternative for adolescents aged 12 years or older. Nucleoside analogues with a low barrier to resistance, such as lamivudine, adefovir, or telbivudine, are not recommended due to the risk of drug resistance. Treatment for Children Aged 2–11 Years Current evidence is insufficient to extend the same treatment eligibility criteria used for adults and adolescents to children aged 2–11 years. Treatment is generally offered on a case-by-case basis to selected children with cirrhosis, advanced liver fibrosis (≥F2), persistent hepatitis flares with HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL, or comorbidities that increase the risk of progressive liver disease. These comorbidities may include co-infections (e.g., HIV, HCV, HDV), iron overload, or the need for immunosuppressive therapy. Global Prevalence and Transmission of CHB The highest prevalence of CHB among children is observed in sub-Saharan Africa and certain Asian countries. Vertical mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) is the most common mode of HBV transmission globally, accounting for most new infections in children under five years old. Horizontal transmission (e.g., child-to-child or household transmission) is also common in regions with poor infection control practices. Evidence for Antiviral Therapy in Adolescents Systematic reviews of antiviral therapy in adolescents with CHB have shown that treatment with TDF, ETV, or TAF effectively reduces HBV DNA levels, normalizes ALT, and achieves HBeAg seroconversion. However, most studies focused on adolescents with very high baseline viral loads (>2 million IU/mL), and there is limited evidence on long-term clinical outcomes such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) or cirrhosis. Safety and Monitoring Antiviral therapy for adolescents is generally safe, but long-term safety data are limited. TDF has been associated with reductions in bone mineral density and increased creatinine levels in some studies. The long-term effects on bone and kidney health in children remain unclear. TAF may be associated with weight gain and hyperlipidemia in adults, but its safety profile in children is not yet fully established. Hepatitis flares may occur after discontinuing nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy, particularly with unplanned treatment interruptions during adolescence. Careful monitoring and adherence support are essential to mitigate these risks. Expanding Treatment to Adolescents Expanding treatment to include adolescents with CHB is particularly relevant in sub-Saharan Africa, where a significant proportion of the population is under 20 years old, and HBV birth-dose vaccination coverage is low. Treating adolescent girls of reproductive age may reduce vertical and horizontal transmission to infants, addressing a major route of HBV transmission globally. Conclusion While treatment for children under 12 years remains on a case-by-case basis, the updated guidelines recommend expanded and simplified treatment eligibility for adolescents. This approach aligns with adult treatment recommendations and aims to reduce the burden of CHB, improve liver health, and prevent long-term complications such as cirrhosis and HCC.
